Article Title: 'Power Banks' for satellites? Bengaluru Company builds tech to keep ageing spacecraft alive
Article Text:
Aule On-screen setup running multibody dynamics simulations and tracking system capturing hardware test data for position and velocity for correlation

Aule 2: Dark room hardware test setup where the team recreated on-orbit lighting conditions with a sun simulator and a target mounted on a robotic arm to simulate the target’s motion.

BENGALURU: What if satellites could simply plug into a power bank instead of drifting away when they run out of fuel? That’s the idea driving a Bengaluru startup building “jetpack” satellites designed to latch onto ageing spacecraft, take over their propulsion duties and keep billion-dollar assets working years longer.After recently validating a key part of its technology at an Isro facility used for India’s SpaDeX docking mission, Aule Space is now preparing for what could become one of the world’s most ambitious private satellite docking demonstrations.For satellite operators, running out of fuel doesn’t necessarily mean spacecraft have reached the end of life. In many cases, expensive communication satellites remain fully functional, but can no longer maintain their assigned orbital positions because they have exhausted the propellant needed for station-keeping. Once that happens, operators are forced to retire assets worth hundreds of millions of dollars.Aule has found another way. “We’re trying to build satellites which can go and dock to existing satellites in space which don’t have any installed ports... and extend their life so that they can keep generating revenue,” CEO Jay Panchal, told TOI. “It’s like a power bank,” he added.Instead of attempting the far more complicated task of refuelling satellites in orbit, Aule’s approach is to send a smaller “jetpack” spacecraft that docks with an existing communications satellite and assumes responsibility for station-keeping using its own propulsion system.The company plans to target geostationary communication satellites, many of which cost more than $300 million to build and generate significant annual revenues.The challenge lies in docking with satellites that were never designed to be serviced. Rather than relying on dedicated docking ports, Aule will attach its spacecraft to the liquid apogee motor (LAM) nozzle, a standard external feature found on most geostationary satellites.If successful, the technology could help operators extract years of additional service from satellites that would otherwise become orbital relics. Panchal said each docked “jetpack” could extend a satellite’s operational life by up to 5 years.*Key Test Done*The startup recently completed a major milestone by testing its camera-based guidance, navigation and control system at the Rendezvous Simulation Laboratory (RSL) at Isro’s ISITE — the same lab where critical elements of the SpaDeX were validated.“We were the first non-govt entity to access RSL. This is the best kind of on-ground testing we can do for these capabilities,” Panchal said.One of Aule’s differentiators is its reliance on computer vision instead of multiple specialised sensors. Current docking systems typically use LiDAR, infrared cameras and other sensors. Aule says its spacecraft will perform the critical final approach using a single optical camera powered by onboard AI.The visual navigation models are trained using data generated in its own facilities and validated at Isro’s testbed before being deployed in orbit.The company is targeting an in-orbit demonstration next year, when it plans to launch two satellites that will autonomously dock in low-Earth orbit. Panchal claims it could be the world’s first private mission to perform non-cooperative docking in LEO using camera-only navigation. The mission will validate technologies that Aule ultimately intends to deploy around geostationary communication satellites.
Article Summary: Bengaluru startup building ‘jetpack’ satellites designed to latch onto ageing spacecraft. Aule Space preparing for what could become one of the world’s most ambitious private satellite docking demonstrations. Company plans to target geostationary communication satellites, many of which cost more than $300 million to build.

Article Title: Scientists use AI to create new viruses; bringing worries of the tech creating biological weapons, deadly poisons and unstoppable pandemics
Article Text:
An atomic reconstruction of one of the bacteriophages designed by the Evo AI model. (Image credit: Samuel H. King et al.)

How AI learned to write DNA like it writes sentences

How scientists confirmed the AI-designed viruses were actually alive

What the researchers did to keep this from going wrong

The gap between what AI can do and what anyone regulates

Poll Vote & Share your view What fascinates you most about AI designing organisms? Potential for medical breakthroughs The technology behind it The ethical implications The novelty of the concept 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Scientists have used artificial intelligence to design viruses that exist nowhere in nature, and 16 of them turned out to be fully functional killers of bacteria. The work, published Thursday in the journal Science by a team at Stanford University and the Arc Institute in California, is the first time an AI model has written the complete instruction manual for a living thing rather than just one piece of it. The viruses in question only attack bacteria and cannot infect people, animals or plants.That last bit is the reassuring part, and everyone involved knows how thin it sounds. The same study that promises a new weapon against superbugs also proves that software trained on DNA can now dream up a working virus from a blank page. Two researchers at Johns Hopkins, Thomas Inglesby and Moritz Hanke, put it plainly in a commentary published alongside it: the ability to write viral genomes with AI now exists, and the rules to control it do not.The models, called Evo 1 and Evo 2, work a lot like ChatGPT. ChatGPT guesses which word comes next. Evo guesses which chemical letter comes next in a strand of DNA, which uses an alphabet of just four letters: A, C, G and T. Feed it enough genetic code and it starts picking up the grammar of life the way a chatbot picks up English.The team, led by Stanford's Brian Hie, trained it on millions of natural genomes, then focused it on one very well-studied virus called ΦX174 and its relatives.Evo spat out hundreds of thousands of possible designs. The researchers picked around 300, had the DNA physically made in a lab, and slipped it into bacteria—which obediently read the instructions and built the viruses themselves.Graduate student Samuel King spotted it in the early hours of the morning. Bacteria growing on a petri dish form a cloudy film, and when a virus is chewing through them, clear spots appear. The spots appeared. When he told the rest of the team, Hie recalls, "the room spontaneously burst into applause."The 16 that survived were not weak imitations. Some multiplied faster than the natural virus they were modelled on. And in the most useful result of the lot, a mix of the AI-designed viruses wiped out E. coli that had already learned to resist the natural version. A comparable mix of viruses collected from nature could not. Bacteria evolve to survive whatever we throw at them—this suggests we can now design new threats faster than they can adapt.They kept anything dangerous out of the training data. No viruses that infect humans, animals, plants or fungi went in, so the model has never seen what a human pathogen looks like. They used a harmless strain of E. coli and worked in a secure lab. Hanke called the caution commendable, while noting the team had no official rulebook to follow.A new US health policy issued last week bans making biological agents more dangerous, but it doesn't cover work done on a computer. And Evo 2 is open source, free for anyone to download, which has alarmed plenty of people.Others say the panic is early. Tom Ellis at Imperial College London called this the smallest, simplest genome anyone could have attempted. Size backs him up: this virus needs about 5,400 letters of code. The simplest living cell needs 500,000. Hie says going bigger would be "a lot of work, but not impossible"—which isn't exactly comforting.
Article Summary: Scientists have used artificial intelligence to design viruses that exist nowhere in nature. 16 of them turned out to be fully functional killers of bacteria. The work is the first time an AI model has written the complete instruction manual for a living thing. The viruses in question only attack bacteria and cannot infect people, animals or plants.

Article Title: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's $450 million superyacht hides a secret sea cabin deep inside the hull, designed to reduce seasickness and ensure peaceful sleep during rough voyages
Article Text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud’s 439-foot Serene one of the most fascinating bedrooms sits three decks below the owner’s suite.

Using naval design to reduce motion

The Balinese inspired cabin. Image – charterworld

Simple Balinese design with practical features

Designer Pascale Reymond once described it as one of the yacht’s coolest ideas (Image – charter​world)

Italian craftsmanship and luxury features

To escape the scorching summer heat of the Middle East, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud equipped his $450 million superyacht Serene with a custom-built snow room cooled to minus 11 degrees Celsius. But despite the yacht's luxurious features, one of its most important design elements is hidden three decks below the main owner's suite.Located near the exact centre of the 439-foot yacht, a secret Balinese-inspired "sea cabin" was specially designed to reduce seasickness and provide a peaceful place to sleep during rough sea journeys.While many billionaire yacht owners place their master bedrooms high up for the best views, Serene has a two-master layout based on how ships move. Reports have long linked the Crown Prince to seasickness during long trips across the Mediterranean and open oceans. Instead of relying only on the yacht's powerful stabilisers, the designers used the science of ship movement to create a calmer sleeping space when the sea becomes rough.The sea cabin is located on the starboard side near the middle of Deck Two, one of the most stable positions on the 134-metre yacht.Naval architecture explains why this location is so effective during voyages. The front of a ship rises and falls heavily in waves, while the rear is affected by pitching, engine vibrations and movement caused by the propellers. Higher decks also move much more from side to side as the yacht rolls.By placing the cabin low in the hull near the centre, the room stays close to the yacht's natural balance points, where movement is at its lowest. Serene is fitted with advanced active stabilisers that greatly reduce rolling, but no system can remove all movement during storms or long ocean crossings. For people who suffer from seasickness, sleeping in the middle of the yacht can make a significant difference.Inside, the sea cabin focuses on calm, simple luxury rather than flashy decoration, creating the feel of a tropical beach retreat. A double bed faces the rear of the yacht beneath a ceiling designed to look like the underside of a traditional Balinese thatched roof. Natural colours, modern furnishings and a floor-to-ceiling headboard separate the bedroom from the open bathroom.One of the cabin's standout features is a large shell door built into the side of the yacht. When Serene is anchored, the door folds down to become a private balcony at sea level, allowing guests to step directly onto the water. During voyages, the balcony stays securely closed, allowing the cabin to serve its main purpose as a stable bedroom.Designer Pascale Reymond once described the cabin as one of the yacht's best ideas because "it's so earthy." Its location is also highly practical. A guest kitchen sits next door, allowing the owner to prepare a late-night snack without calling crew members or climbing several flights of stairs. The spa and beach club are just a short walk away, while a private lift connects the cabin directly to the main owner's suite on Deck Five. This gives the Crown Prince a spacious suite for relaxing in calm waters and a quieter, more stable room for sleeping at sea.Built by Italian shipyard Fincantieri and launched in 2011, Serene is one of the largest and most advanced superyachts ever constructed in Italy. The yacht measures 439 feet (134 metres) long with a beam of 60.7 feet (18.5 metres). Its exterior was designed by Espen Øino, while the interiors were created by Reymond Langton Design. According to Charter World, Serene is powered by eight MTU 4000-series engines, cruises comfortably at 15 knots, reaches a top speed of 20 knots, accommodates 24 guests in 12 cabins, and is operated by a crew of 52.Besides its special sea cabin, Serene offers an impressive range of luxury facilities across seven decks. The yacht has two helicopter landing pads, one of which can be turned into a swimming pool or dance floor, a submarine hangar, and an underwater viewing lounge called the Nemo Room, inspired by Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.To help guests escape the region's extreme heat, the yacht also includes a snow room cooled to around 12 degrees Fahrenheit (-11°C). The room creates real falling snow, allowing guests to move directly into a nearby sauna, hammam, steam room or heated spa pools. With an indoor seawater swimming pool, an outdoor cinema, a piano lounge and domed fireplaces, Serene combines luxury with smart engineering to handle both extreme heat and rough seas.
Article Summary: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud's 439-foot superyacht Serene has a secret Balinese-inspired "sea cabin" The cabin was designed to reduce seasickness and provide a peaceful place to sleep during rough sea journeys. It is located on the starboard side near the middle of Deck Two, one of the most stable positions on the 134-metre yacht.

Article Title: Apple releases macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 to fix Screen Sharing security flaw
Article Text:
Mac users can check for the latest update in the Settings app

How to download macOS Tahoe 26.6.1

Apple's most popular Mac is now its hardest to buy

Apple has released macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, a new security update for Mac users that fixes a vulnerability related to the Screen Sharing feature. According to Apple’s security support document, the flaw could allow an attacker to authenticate to Screen Sharing without having valid credentials. Apple says it has addressed the security issue by improving state management. The company has also released updates for older macOS versions, including macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 and macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, with the same security fix.The fix is not limited to Macs running macOS Tahoe. Apple has also released macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 and macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, which address the same Screen Sharing vulnerability. This means Mac users who have not upgraded to macOS Tahoe can also install the security fix while remaining on their existing supported macOS version.Mac users can check for the latest update by opening the System Settings app and navigating to the Software Update section. If macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 is available for the device, users can download and install it from there.Given that the update addresses a security vulnerability that could allow authentication without valid credentials, users may want to install the latest available update on their Macs.In another news, shipping estimates of Apple MacBook Air have slipped by weeks across nearly every configuration, likely because of the global memory shortage. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in his Power On newsletter that retail sources describe Air inventory as more constrained than they can ever recall. Order a base model from Apple's online store today and delivery lands at the end of August. Buyers of the Apple MacBook Air are reportedly being told to wait till early September to get hold of the device.
Article Summary: macOS Tahoe 26.6.1 is a new security update for Mac users that fixes a vulnerability related to the Screen Sharing feature. The flaw could allow an attacker to authenticate to Screen Sharing without having valid credentials. Apple has also released updates for older macOS versions, including macOS Sonoma 14.8.9 and macOS Sequoia 15.7.9.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Michel Foucault: 'Maybe the target nowadays is not to discover what we are but to refuse what we are' and how every self-help guru got it wrong
Article Text:
Michel Foucault was a French philosopher and historian whose work explored how power, knowledge and social institutions shape human behaviour, identity and society.

"Maybe the target nowadays is not to discover what we are but to refuse what we are."

An essay for a changing world

The Subject and Power

,

How identity is created

Why the idea matters today

The Subject and Power

In 1971, during a televised debate hosted by Dutch philosopher Fons Elders, French philosopher Michel Foucault sat across from linguist Noam Chomsky. Chomsky argued that human beings have a natural, universal human nature that political systems should help develop. Foucault disagreed completely. He argued that what society calls "human nature" is often created by powerful institutions to classify, control and manage people.More than a decade later, Foucault summed up this idea in a single statement:The quote challenges the common belief that people should "find themselves." Instead of looking inward for a true, fixed identity, Foucault argues that many of the labels shaping our identity, including medical diagnoses, gender roles, consumer identities and political categories, are created by society rather than by ourselves. In this view, freedom comes not from discovering a hidden self but from questioning and rejecting the labels placed upon us.The quote comes from Foucault's 1982 essay "" published in the academic journal Critical Inquiry. Written near the end of his life, the essay brings together decades of his research on prisons, psychiatric hospitals, medicine and sexuality.By the early 1980s, Western societies had moved away from the open displays of power seen in earlier centuries.Governments no longer relied mainly on public punishments to control people. Instead, power became quieter and worked through institutions and administration. Foucault argued that modern power mainly operates by shaping individual identity. Institutions tell people who they are, whether as a patient, a criminal, a consumer or a productive worker.Writing for political theorists and social scientists, Foucault argued that the biggest struggle of the modern age was no longer only against religion or economic inequality. It was also against systems of power that define people's identities and expect both individuals and society to accept those identities as truth.The quote is correctly attributed to Foucault. The Subject and Power remains one of his most widely cited works and explains many of his later ideas about power and resistance.To understand Foucault's philosophy, it is important to understand his idea of "subjectification" (assujettissement). In French, the word has two meanings. It describes becoming an independent individual while also becoming controlled by others.Since the Enlightenment, many Western philosophers believed that discovering the truth about yourself leads to freedom. René Descartes searched for certainty through the thinking mind, while Sigmund Freud explored the unconscious to understand human behaviour. Foucault challenged this tradition. He argued that when people receive psychological diagnoses, attend therapy or complete surveys, they are taking part in systems that define what is considered normal and abnormal.In Foucault's view, knowledge and power cannot be separated. When medicine defines mental health, or economics defines a successful citizen, those definitions also create social boundaries. People then begin to judge themselves according to those standards.Refusing what we are becomes a way of resisting these institutional limits. Instead of asking, "Who am I?", Foucault asks, "How has society shaped who I am, and how can I move beyond those limits?" His thinking builds on Immanuel Kant's idea that people should think for themselves. It also adds another challenge. We should question the ideas and categories that society gives us.More than four decades after Foucault wrote, his ideas seem especially relevant in today's digital world.In 2026, technology companies and artificial intelligence systems collect huge amounts of personal data. Algorithms study browsing history, location, typing habits and shopping behaviour to build detailed profiles of each user. These systems predict what people will buy, what opinions they may hold and even which communities they belong to. Social media often rewards people for fitting into these digital identities, creating echo chambers that reinforce them.When people accept these algorithm-created profiles as their true identity, they reflect the concern Foucault raised. Applying his ideas today means questioning these categories instead of simply accepting them. It may mean rejecting a workplace culture that measures personal worth only through productivity, or treating a mental health diagnosis as a useful medical tool instead of allowing it to become a person's entire identity.For Foucault, refusing an imposed identity is not about withdrawing from society. It is an active choice to resist allowing institutions to decide what a person's life should be.Foucault never offered a perfect vision of what people should become after rejecting these labels. Instead, he believed freedom is an ongoing process of questioning the identities and definitions handed down by authority while creating space to live beyond them.
Article Summary: Michel Foucault was a French philosopher and historian. His work explored how power, knowledge and social institutions shape human behaviour, identity and society. He argued that what society calls "human nature" is often created by powerful institutions to classify, control and manage people. His ideas seem especially relevant in today's digital world.

Article Title: Quote of the day by JS Mill: 'I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than...' and the 19th-century cure for modern burnout
Article Text:
John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind

I have learned to seek my happiness by limiting my desires, rather than in attempting to satisfy them.”

The breakdown of a calculating mind

The utilitarian paradox

Curbing the engine of infinite wants

A shopper standing in the middle of a brightly lit superstore, holding three slightly different versions of the same household item, often feels an odd sense of confusion rather than freedom. The endless scroll of online stores promises that the perfect product to complete life is just one click away. Yet, as packages keep arriving at the door, the promised happiness often disappears, replaced by a lingering desire for whatever comes next.This cycle of endless consumption is exactly what the Victorian philosopher John Stuart Mill described when he wrote: “Mill’s observation completely changes the usual idea of finding happiness. Instead of seeing human desire as an endless list of needs that must be fulfilled, he argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Satisfaction, in his view, does not come from building a bigger net to catch every passing impulse, but from reducing what we expect and demand from the world.John Stuart Mill published this reflection in his Autobiography in 1873, a book describing one of the most intense intellectual upbringings in Western history.Born in London in 1806, Mill was raised under a strict educational experiment designed by his father, James Mill, and the founder of Utilitarianism, Jeremy Bentham. By the age of three, he was learning Ancient Greek; by eight, he was reading Herodotus and Plato in their original language; and by his early teens, he had mastered political economy and formal logic.The purpose of this education was to create a perfectly rational follower of Bentham—a person trained to judge every action by calculating how to produce the greatest pleasure and the least pain for the greatest number of people.The experiment seemed successful until 1826, when twenty-year-old Mill suffered a serious mental breakdown. In one of the most famous parts of his memoir, Mill recalled asking himself a simple question: if all his political and social goals were achieved tomorrow, would he truly feel happy? His honest answer was an immediate “no.” His highly rational way of thinking had left him emotionally empty.Mill’s recovery happened gradually, helped by the poetry of William Wordsworth and by a major reconsideration of Utilitarian philosophy. He realized that Bentham’s basic idea—treating happiness as simply the total of fulfilled desires—was deeply incomplete. To recover his peace of mind, Mill had to rethink what true well-being meant. The quotation from his Autobiography marks this important turning point, showing his realization that lasting happiness comes from controlling desire rather than satisfying every new craving.To understand Mill’s change in thinking, we must examine a tension within Utilitarian philosophy. Traditional Utilitarianism viewed happiness as the total amount of pleasure minus pain. If people could continue creating and satisfying new desires, happiness should, in theory, continue increasing.Mill recognized the major problem with this idea: human desires constantly grow. As soon as one desire is fulfilled, our expectations rise again, a pattern that modern psychologists call the “hedonic treadmill.” Trying to find lasting happiness by satisfying every new want is like trying to fill a bucket full of holes.By encouraging people to limit their desires, Mill was not promoting extreme self-denial or the lifestyle of monks. Instead, he brought his updated version of Utilitarianism closer to older philosophical traditions. Epicurus had argued centuries earlier that simple, easily achieved pleasures bring the greatest peace of mind, while Stoic thinkers such as Seneca believed that true wealth comes not from owning many things, but from wanting fewer things.Mill adapted this idea for the modern industrial world. He argued that higher intellectual and emotional pleasures—such as art, friendship, public service, and personal development—are naturally more valuable than endlessly collecting material possessions. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness that do not lose their value once they are achieved.In 2026, Mill’s insight speaks directly to one of the biggest challenges of modern life: the commercialization of human attention and desire. Today’s digital systems are carefully designed to constantly create new wants that can only be satisfied through more consumption. Targeted algorithms, personalized advertising, and micro-influencers work together to convince people that something important is always missing from their lives.The growing popularity of voluntary simplicity, digital minimalism, and anti-consumption movements reflects Mill’s principle in action. When technology workers switch to basic feature phones or consumers commit to “no-buy” years, they are putting his idea into practice. They are not doing so because they lack money, but because they want to break the endless cycle of constantly creating new desires.The same principle also applies to work and professional burnout. Modern workplaces often define success through constant growth: higher salaries, bigger teams, and continuous promotions. However, research in behavioral economics consistently shows that once people reach a comfortable middle-class standard of living, extra income brings smaller and smaller increases in everyday happiness. Executives who reject promotions to protect their personal lives or professionals who choose lower-paying jobs for better health are deciding to reduce their ambitions rather than spend their lives chasing ever-growing demands.By describing happiness as the relationship between what people have and what they want, Mill offered a lasting mathematical insight: the result can be improved either by increasing what you have or by reducing what you want.When Mill died in Avignon in 1873, he left behind writings that influenced modern liberal democracy, individual freedom, and economic thought. Yet perhaps his greatest personal achievement was overcoming the crisis of his youth. By understanding that peace of mind depends on controlling desire instead of constantly feeding it, he left a timeless guide for staying mentally balanced in a world designed to keep people forever wanting more.
Article Summary: John Stuart Mill was a 19th-century philosopher who argued that true happiness comes from developing the mind. He argued that desire itself is what needs to be controlled. Limiting material and superficial desires frees mental energy, allowing people to develop deeper, non-material sources of happiness.

Article Title: Mountain lions may be making roads safer in Washington, because deer change their behaviour when pumas are nearby, and collisions drop
Article Text:
New research indicates mountain lions reduce deer-vehicle collisions significantly. Predator presence makes deer avoid roads and developed areas more often. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Large carnivores shape

road safety

through effects on prey space use

How mountain lions influence deer movement

This behavioural shift lowers the likelihood of dangerous animal-vehicle encounters. The study examined deer movement and collision data in Washington's Olympic Peninsula. These findings highlight the broader ecological roles of large carnivores. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

A reminder that predators have wider roles in ecosystems

For drivers in forested areas, deer on the road can be unpredictable and dangerous. Wildlife warning signs and speed restrictions are common reminders of this risk, but new research suggests that nature itself may play a role in reducing these collisions. Mountain lions, also called pumas or cougars, are often discussed for their impact on wildlife and for concerns about human encounters. But a study suggests they may have another indirect effect. By changing how deer move through their surroundings, mountain lions may reduce the chances of deer entering areas where vehicles and wildlife often collide.The findings come from a study published in Current Biology titled. The research examined how the presence of mountain lions influenced deer behaviour and deer-vehicle collisions in Washington's Olympic Peninsula. The researchers combined camera trap data from around 500 locations and GPS collar data from approximately 60 mountain lions with records of deer-vehicle collisions to examine how predator presence influenced deer movement and collision risk.The researchers wanted to know more than whether mountain lions reduce deer numbers. They looked at a different question: can predators change the way prey animals use a landscape even when they are not directly hunting them? Mountain lions are predators that can influence deer behaviour through the risk they pose as hunters.They often stalk animals quietly before making a sudden attack from a close distance. Areas where forests meet open spaces, including roads and developed areas, can provide opportunities for these hunting strategies. These same places are also locations where deer often come into contact with vehicles.The researchers found that deer in areas with mountain lions spent less time near roads and developed areas and more time in wooded habitats. The findings suggest that the presence of predators influenced how deer used the landscape, reducing the time they spent in places where encounters with vehicles were more likely.The researchers reported that deer in areas with mountain lions were 86% more likely to spend time farther from roads and development, indicating that predator presence was linked to changes in how deer used the landscape. These behavioural changes were associated with fewer deer-vehicle collisions. The researchers estimated that areas with mountain lions had a lower risk of deer-vehicle collisions, with the models predicting a 67% reduction in collision likelihood and a 76% reduction in expected collisions over five years within the study area. In this case, mountain lions appear to improve road safety indirectly. They are not preventing crashes by controlling traffic or physically keeping deer away from roads. Instead, their presence changes the choices deer make about where they spend time.The relationship between predators and prey is more complicated than one species eating another. Large carnivores can influence ecosystems through a range of effects, including changes in movement patterns, habitat use and interactions between different species. The Current Biology study adds to research showing that predators can shape how animals use landscapes. The authors focused on the indirect effects of mountain lions, showing how their presence may affect human concerns such as road safety.Deer movement is shaped by several ecological factors, and the relationship between predators, prey behaviour and roads can vary across landscapes. The researchers noted that more work is needed to understand how these effects change under different conditions.The study also offers a different way of viewing animals that are often considered only through the lens of conflict. Mountain lions can sometimes create challenges for communities, especially where human development overlaps with wildlife habitat. But their role in ecosystems can also produce benefits that are not immediately obvious.Understanding these connections may help conservationists and communities make better decisions about sharing space with wildlife. Protecting predators is not only about maintaining biodiversity. It can also involve recognising the quieter ways these animals influence the environment around them.For people driving through regions where mountain lions and deer live, a safer road may seem like it should come only from human solutions. Yet this research shows that natural relationships can also shape everyday experiences. A predator moving through a forest can influence where another animal chooses to travel, and that choice can eventually affect what happens on nearby roads.
Article Summary: Study examined deer movement and collision data in Washington's Olympic Peninsula. Deer in areas with mountain lions were 86% more likely to spend time farther from roads and development. Predator presence makes deer avoid roads and developed areas more often. These behavioural changes were associated with fewer deer-vehicle collisions.

Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Article Title: AI is in finance, but is it ready? 76% firms use AI as governance lags, says report
Article Text:
Only 28% are reassessing the talent profiles needed for an AI-driven finance workforce.

Better AI needs better data

AI is becoming a bigger part of finance departments, but companies are finding that adopting the technology is easier than figuring out how people, data and controls should work around it.A KPMG report found that 76 per cent of organisations are already using AI in financial planning. Yet the report suggests that simply adding AI tools will not be enough to create an advantage. The bigger gains are expected to come from using AI to support better financial decisions, while building the systems and governance needed to manage its growing role."Competitive advantage will increasingly belong to organizations that align their finance operating model around AI -- and can sustain that alignment as AI becomes more capable, more autonomous and more deeply embedded in everyday decision-making."The shift is also exposing a gap in how companies are preparing their finance teams.While 38 per cent of organisations are upskilling finance and internal audit employees for AI-enabled processes, only 28 per cent are hiring for new skill sets. An identical 28 per cent are reassessing the talent profiles they will need as AI becomes more deeply integrated into finance.In other words, most organisations are teaching their existing workforce to use AI rather than redesigning the workforce around human-AI collaboration.That transition is also keeping humans firmly in the loop. KPMG found that 33 per cent of organisations are increasing human oversight specifically because of concerns linked to AI.This remains particularly important in finance, where decisions can involve regulatory requirements and professional judgement. Human checks, the report said, can make AI-driven outputs more reliable while helping organisations build confidence in the technology.Even as companies expand AI use, the quality of the underlying data remains a major constraint.About 36 per cent of organisations identified better data quality, integration and interoperability between systems as the biggest opportunity to get more value from AI in finance.The challenge, therefore, is not simply having more AI tools. Finance teams also need to understand which data can be trusted, how AI-generated outputs should be interpreted and how those findings can be translated into decisions."Data fluency is emerging as the most critical capability need: the ability to assess data quality, interpret outputs and communicate findings in terms the business can act on."The report's broader takeaway is that AI adoption alone may not determine which finance teams benefit most. Companies that combine the technology with stronger governance, appropriate talent and reliable data are likely to be better placed as AI becomes more autonomous.
Article Summary: KPMG: 76% of organisations are already using AI in financial planning. Only 28% are reassessing the talent profiles needed for an AI-driven finance workforce. Companies that combine the technology with stronger governance, appropriate talent and reliable data will benefit most.

Article Title: Before the knowledge walks out the door
Article Text:
Everyone in Silicon Valley is racing to build machines that replace human expertise.

Ahmer Inam

, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it.

When Ahmer Inam appeared on Fox & Friends in June, his mother watched the segment without following much of it. Her English is limited. There was her son on the famous curved couch of American morning television, fielding questions about artificial intelligence, and she understood almost none of the words. She wept anyway. Some distances need no translation, and the one between a schoolteacher's household in Delhi and a Manhattan television studio is legible in any language.Had she followed the argument, it might have surprised her less than it surprised the audience. Because what Inam was defending, underneath the vocabulary of frontier AI, is approximately the oldest idea in civilisation — the one his father practised for a living: that knowledge survives only when one generation troubles to hand it to the next.Inam has spent twenty-five years building artificial intelligence — long enough to remember when it meant symbolic logic in the late nineties, and senior enough to have run AI and data for Fortune 500 companies, Nike and Wells Fargo among them, back when "chief AI officer" was still an exotic title. He is not, in other words, a critic sniping from the cheap seats. Which makes the thesis of Cognisee, the research lab he founded and leads, sound almost seditious in today's Silicon Valley: "We're not trying to replace the worker," he says."We're trying to make the worker irreplaceable."The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage." By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030 — electricians, welders, machinists, the hands America needs if it is serious about building factories, chip plants and grid capacity again. But Inam's diagnosis is sharper than a headcount. "America does not have a work shortage," he likes to say. "It has an expertise shortage."Consider what actually leaves the building when a master electrician retires at sixty-eight. Not the manual — the manual stays. What leaves is the ear that catches a motor running slightly wrong two weeks before it fails; the instinct that connects a faint vibration to a pattern in old maintenance logs; forty years of judgment that was never written down because it could not be. The philosopher Michael Polanyi had a name for this — tacit knowledge, the things we know but cannot tell — and Cognisee is, at bottom, a bet that the most valuable training data on earth is tacit.The company's method has a fable-like symmetry. Its AI begins as an apprentice: it works alongside experienced people and learns what they notice, what they ask, how they make judgment calls. Then it turns around and becomes a coach, carrying that accumulated judgment to the newcomer. "First it's an apprentice," Inam says. "Then it becomes a coach." Picture a 22-year-old on his first aircraft-maintenance job, hearing a sound he has never heard before, with the distilled instincts of the country's best technicians beside him in real time. "He's not being replaced by a machine," Inam says. "He's being mentored by one."The repository where all this lives is called, a little grandly, a Wisdom Vault — a secure library of hard-won know-how from doctors, nurses, electricians, factory workers, farmers, small-business owners. Grand or not, the name gives away the emotional register Inam is working in. This is not pitched as workforce optimisation. It is pitched as inheritance.He is careful — insistent, actually — about the question that framing invites: who owns it? In Cognisee's design, the expert decides what to preserve, what to share, and with whom; the contributor is recognised and rewarded; the knowledge belongs to the person who earned it, not to the machine that absorbed it. "There is a big difference," Inam says, "between being monitored and being mentored." The company is incorporated as a public benefit corporation, which he describes as a legal commitment to the worker rather than a marketing pledge.That ownership principle is also where his quarrel with the reigning AI paradigm becomes explicit. The frontier labs, Inam argues, got intelligent by swallowing the written internet — and the written internet is now substantially swallowed, which is why the industry's plan increasingly amounts to bigger data centres and more electricity, even as some of the field's own pioneers warn of a wall ahead. His contrarian wager is that the next leap will come not from more compute but from the knowledge that never made it onto the internet in the first place — and that it can be gathered by consent rather than by crawler.For an Indian reader, the resonance is hard to miss. This is a country that has watched its weaves, its remedies and its craft knowledge catalogued, carried off and sold back to it before. It is also a country whose deepest teaching traditions were never textual at all, but moved from person to person — the guru-shishya parampara, the ustad and the shagird. Inam has spoken about Wisdom Vaults for indigenous and medicinal knowledge, with communities retaining ownership of what they contribute. One way to describe Cognisee is as an attempt to give the world's oral inheritances an infrastructure layer — sovereignty included.The idea is attracting converts from unexpected quarters. Cognisee's co-founder, Alex Giannou, spent nearly two decades on Wall Street financing precisely the data centres and power deals behind the AI boom; he crossed over, in Inam's telling, because the right bet and the smart bet turned out to be the same one. Among the company's early backers is a senior Google executive who helped invent federated learning, one of the foundational privacy-preserving techniques of modern machine learning. And last year the XPRIZE Foundation, where Inam serves as a Visionary, recognised his work with its Global Visioneering Award.None of which quite explains the conviction. For that you have to go back to Delhi. Inam grew up in a low-income household, the son of a teacher — a man who spent his working life on the least scalable expertise-transfer technology ever devised: one adult, one room, one generation at a time. The son's journey to America was not gilded; there were stretches, early on, when he could not always afford to eat. It takes a particular kind of person to emerge from that and conclude that a nation's most undervalued asset sits not in its server farms but in the heads of its retiring machinists and nurses."Every generation should start where the last one left off," Inam says. It sounds like a product principle. It is closer to a family creed — the thing his father practised without ever calling it a thesis, the thing his mother recognised on a television screen in a language she does not speak. Some knowledge, it turns out, transfers just fine.
Article Summary: Ahmer Inam, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it. The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage" By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030.

What's on offer



How subscribers can access it



Spotify has rolled out Premium Rewards in India, a new limited-edition initiative that gives Premium subscribers access to curated brand offers and invite-only live experiences, the company announced on Wednesday. The move adds a lifestyle and events layer on top of the music streaming service's existing offering of high-quality, ad-free, offline listening.Premium Rewards is built around two categories of benefits. The first is lifestyle perks — exclusive offers from partner brands including MakeMyTrip, Tira, Nykaa, Ajio Luxe, Gully Labs and Airbnb, spanning travel, beauty, fashion and lifestyle categories. The second is what Spotify is calling "IRL experiences": invite-only events, intimate listening sessions and cultural moments designed to give subscribers closer access to artists and music.Spotify says the rewards are curated around how subscribers actually live, travel and shop, positioning the initiative less as a set of discount coupons and more as an extension of the value of being a Premium member.Premium Rewards is available through a dedicated microsite, premiumrewards.byspotify.com, where Premium subscribers can browse available rewards and claim offers directly. She said Premium has always centered on delivering the best audio experience — high quality, uninterrupted listening with offline access — and that Premium Rewards is meant to carry that same feeling into subscribers' everyday lives, the brands they engage with and the experiences they remember. She described the goal as making Premium function more like a membership than a plain subscription, adding that the rewards are being offered as a limited-edition experience for now, making the present moment a particularly good time to be a Premium subscriber in India.

Article Title: In September 2025, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman outlined a clear red line for AI, said: AI must be shut down immediately if it ever gains …
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman

‘AI’s four fatal capabilities’

“So those are the four criteria: Recursive self-improvement, setting its own goals, acquiring its own resources, and acting autonomously,

Nuclear-style regulation is not optional

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has outlined a firm “red line” for artificial intelligence (AI) safety, warning that if any AI system displays four specific autonomous capabilities simultaneously, it must be shut down immediately to prevent catastrophic risks. Suleyman cautioned that an AI model operating with these unrestricted capabilities could become so powerful over the next five to ten years that stopping it would require military-grade intervention.In a podcast with Trevor Noah , South African comedian and writer, in September last year, the tech executive said that to prevent such scenarios advanced frontier models must be subjected to strict auditing and oversight similar to the regulations governing critical national infrastructure like nuclear power.According to Suleyman, an AI system crosses a dangerous threshold when it combines four distinct autonomous traits. The first is recursive self-improvement, which is the ability for an AI model to rewrite, modify and optimise its own underlying source code without human input.The second is autonomous goal-setting wherein a system establishes its own objectives independent of programmer instructions. Next is the ability of autonomous action to execute decisions and interact with digital or physical systems without human authorisation.The fourth and final is the capability to independently acquire financial, computational or material resources to support its own operations.Suleyman emphasised that while individual capabilities are being researched across the industry, allowing all four to converge in a single system creates an unmanageable security threat.” Microsoft AI CEO said.Comparing the risks to high-consequence industries, Suleyman argued that developing superintelligent AI cannot remain an unregulated private enterprise.“Just like you can’t just go off and say, ‘I've got a billion dollars. I’m going to go build a nuclear power plant'... it’s a restricted activity because of the one-to-many impact it can have,” Suleyman said, urging industry leaders and governments to embrace formal regulatory frameworks.He added that tech companies and governments must collaborate on strict capability auditing before advanced models are deployed.
Article Summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has outlined a firm ‘red line’ for artificial intelligence (AI) safety. He warned that if any AI system displays four specific autonomous capabilities simultaneously, it must be shut down immediately. Sulyman cautioned that an AI model operating with these unrestricted capabilities could become so powerful over the next five to ten years that stopping it would require military-grade intervention.

Article Title: Samsung devices not just top in AI experience, but also provide advantage of ecosystem, OS upgrades and privacy
Article Text:
JB Park highlighted Samsung’s ecosystem as a defining advantage

Samsung is tailoring Galaxy AI to local needs: Jay Kim

India-specific partnerships

As AI features across smartphones increasingly start to look alike, Samsung is betting that its edge over the next few years won't come from AI alone, but from how deeply that intelligence is woven into its broader hardware, software and device ecosystem. That was the central message from JB Park, CEO and President of Samsung Southwest Asia, and Jay Kim, Corporate EVP and Head of the Customer Experience Office at Samsung's MX Division, in a roundtable discussion on the company's AI strategy.Asked what Samsung sees as its defining competitive advantage as AI capabilities converge across the industry, Park pointed to the way AI performs differently depending on the device it runs on. He noted that creative professionals often prefer editing photos and videos on the Galaxy Fold's larger foldable display over a standard bar-type phone, suggesting that AI features gain real value when paired with the right form factor.Beyond hardware, Park argued that Samsung's real strength lies in its ecosystem, which stretches well past phones and watches into home appliances and displays, all linked together so a smartphone becomes the control centre for a connected home.He pointed to AI-driven energy efficiency monitoring for appliances as one example of that connected approach. Park also flagged Samsung's commitment to seven years of OS upgrades and its focus on privacy as factors that set the company apart from rivals, framing these together as the combination that differentiates Samsung from the competition.“I think Samsung is very good in terms of ecosystem. We’re not limited to just phones and watches, but the Samsung ecosystem extends to home appliances and displays that are all linked together. You are at the centre, controlling your home appliances through a smartphone. And, you can monitor as well as make the best in terms of the energy efficiency (for appliances by using AI). We’re giving 7 years of OS upgrades and are focussed on privacy. All these factors differentiate us from competition,” Park told The Times of India.Jay Kim traced Samsung's AI evolution across recent flagship generations. The Galaxy S24, the company's first AI phone, introduced AI features tied to specific services and apps. The Galaxy S25 followed with agentic AI capabilities, including Gemini integration. With the Galaxy S26, Samsung introduced what it describes as the industry's first AI operating system, developed in collaboration with Google, representing a further step in agentic AI where the system can interpret context, automate tasks and proactively surface recommendations before users ask for them.“We're getting a lot of feedback from local markets and we will gradually apply the learnings. But I would say that we're in an early stage in terms of understanding how AI actually helps consumers’ lives every day,” said Kim.Park added that in India, Samsung has partnered with IITs and startups to improve AI usability and consumer journeys. He noted that AI usage in India is higher than the global average, with Galaxy AI features such as Photo Assist, Creative Studio, and Audio Eraser being used nearly twice as often. “In India, the usage of AI by consumers is higher than global average. Galaxy AI features such as Photo Assist, Creative Studio and Audio Eraser are used nearly twice as often as the global average. This is just the beginning of our journey for developing AI use cases in India,” added Park.
