Article Title: Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai: “You might fail a few times, but that’s okay…” - what his words teach us about failure, learning and moving forward
Article Text:
PC: BBC

Quote of the day by Sundar Pichai

“You might fail a few times, but that's okay. You end up doing something worthwhile which you learn a great deal from”

What Sundar Pichai’s words actually mean

Sundar Pichai’s journey from Madurai to Google CEO

Why failure can produce useful information

What to do after failure: Lessons that help you move forward

What was within your control? What was not? Was the problem a lack of preparation, an unrealistic expectation, poor timing or simply an outcome that could not reasonably have been predicted?

Why the message still has relevance

What Sundar Pichai’s quote really teaches us about failure

Failure is not the end: An unsuccessful attempt does not necessarily mean the journey is over.

An unsuccessful attempt does not necessarily mean the journey is over. Every setback can teach you something: Even when things go wrong, the experience may provide useful knowledge for the future.

Even when things go wrong, the experience may provide useful knowledge for the future. Focus on what changed: Instead of asking only whether you succeeded or failed, consider what the experience taught you.

Instead of asking only whether you succeeded or failed, consider what the experience taught you. Learn from your mistakes: A setback can reveal weaknesses in your preparation, planning, timing or decision-making.

A setback can reveal weaknesses in your preparation, planning, timing or decision-making. Be willing to change direction: Failure may show that a particular approach or path is not worth pursuing further.

Failure may show that a particular approach or path is not worth pursuing further. Use experience to make better choices: What you learn from one attempt can influence how you approach the next one.

What you learn from one attempt can influence how you approach the next one. Failure does not guarantee success: Pichai’s words are not a promise that every mistake will eventually produce a positive outcome.

Pichai’s words are not a promise that every mistake will eventually produce a positive outcome. What happens next matters: Failure is simply an outcome; its longer-term value depends on how you respond and what you learn from it.

Failure tends to look much larger when it is happening to you than when you hear about it afterwards. A rejected application, an exam result that falls short or a project that quietly goes nowhere can feel like a dead end. Yet successful careers are rarely made up of clean decisions and predictable outcomes. Sundar Pichai , the Indian-born technology executive who became chief executive of Google and later Alphabet, has spoken about this in fairly plain terms. “You might fail a few times, but that's okay. You end up doing something worthwhile which you learn a great deal from,” he once said. The thought is less about celebrating failure than recognising what can remain after it.There is a tendency to divide experiences into success and failure, as if the two are fixed categories. Pichai’s observation is more useful when viewed as a description of a process.A failed attempt is an outcome. Learning is what comes after it.For instance, someone applying for a job and being turned down.The rejection may reveal very little. Or, after looking back at the interview, the applicant might realise that they struggled to explain their experience clearly. They can work on that before the next interview. The first application has not produced the desired result, but it has supplied something that can be used.The same applies outside work. A student who performs badly in an examination may discover that reading notes repeatedly was not an effective way of preparing. Someone starting a small business may learn that customers were interested in a product but unwilling to pay the planned price. A person learning a new skill may realise that their expectations were unrealistic.None of these situations becomes successful simply because a lesson can be extracted from it. The point is narrower: an unsuccessful outcome does not have to be the end of the useful part of the experience.Sundar Pichai was born in Madurai and grew up in Chennai. He studied metallurgical engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur before moving to the United States for further education, including a master’s degree at Stanford University and an MBA at the Wharton School.He joined Google in 2004. His early work included responsibility for products associated with the company’s toolbar business and later Chrome, the web browser that became one of Google’s most recognisable products.His career inside the company developed over a number of years rather than through one sudden leap. He moved into increasingly senior roles, eventually becoming chief executive of Google in 2015. Four years later, he became chief executive of Alphabet, Google's parent company.That progression matters when considering his comments about failure. His career is often reduced to its most visible milestones, but those milestones were built through a succession of jobs, projects and decisions. A senior executive’s career, like anyone else’s, contains periods where the outcome of a decision cannot be known in advance.There is a practical side to Pichai’s observation. When an attempt succeeds immediately, there may be little incentive to examine every detail of what happened. Failure tends to force a closer look. That examination can be uncomfortable. It may uncover a gap in knowledge or a poor assumption. It can also expose circumstances that were outside a person’s control. Knowing which is which matters.A useful lesson is not necessarily a grand one. Perhaps a presentation needed more preparation. Perhaps an application was aimed at the wrong role. Perhaps a business idea needed testing before money was invested in it. Small discoveries can have a considerable effect when they influence the next decision.There is also a difference between learning from failure and simply experiencing it repeatedly. If the same problem keeps appearing and nothing changes, the setback itself has not taught very much. Pichai’s point depends on the second step: paying attention.The practical response to a setback need not be complicated. It can begin with a straightforward review of what happened.The answers are more useful than simply labelling the experience a failure. For a student, that might mean changing revision methods rather than merely spending more hours studying. For someone looking for employment, it could mean asking whether their applications are reaching the right roles or whether their interview answers need work. In a workplace, a project that did not deliver its intended result might lead to changes in planning, communication or testing.The useful habit is to carry something forward. Even a small adjustment gives the next attempt a different starting point.The pressure to appear successful can make ordinary setbacks feel more unusual than they really are. Professional networking sites, social media profiles and company announcements tend to present finished achievements. They rarely document every abandoned plan or unsuccessful first attempt that preceded them.For students and people early in their careers, that can create an incomplete picture of how progress happens. A CV records qualifications and positions, not every interview that did not work out or every project that was quietly shelved.Pichai’s comment offers a more modest way of looking at those experiences. A setback can be disappointing without being meaningless. It can also be useful without needing to be turned into a success story.That distinction is probably the most practical part of the quote.
Article Summary: Sundar Pichai, the Indian-born technology executive who became chief executive of Google and later Alphabet, has spoken about this in fairly plain terms. “You might fail a few times, but that's okay. You end up doing something worthwhile which you learn a great deal from,” he once said.

Article Title: WhatsApp banned 5.1 million accounts in June: Here’s what can get your account banned
Article Text:
WhatsApp account ban

Why WhatsApp bans an account

What can get your WhatsApp account banned

What a WhatsApp ban actually locks you out of

How to appeal a WhatsApp account ban

Meta recently admitted that a WhatsApp glitch wrongly locked out legitimate users recently, after its automatic content moderation system mistook normal account activity for spam or abusive behaviour. Earlier this month, multiple WhatsApp accounts were put under review for over 24 hours in several countries, prompting affected users to flag the issue on social media. Many reported seeing this message on their screen: "Account in review. Date requested: 3 Aug 2026. Your account activity and device info is being checked to make sure it follows our terms of service. We will notify you of the result typically within 24 hours."In a statement to TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson confirmed the locks were an error, not a rule violation. The spokesperson said the company is constantly trying to identify fraudulent accounts to keep the platform safe, but acknowledged that "mistakes can occur." "Our goal is always to be one step ahead of those who want to abuse our service to ban accounts so that everyone can use it safely, sometimes we miss the mark and when we do, we work to remedy it as soon as possible to get everyone back to chatting," the spokesperson added.The scale of WhatsApp's moderation gives context to how something like this happens. In June alone this year, WhatsApp banned 5.1 million accounts in India — a volume of automated enforcement large enough that legitimate accounts can occasionally get caught in the net alongside genuine bad actors.WhatsApp says it bans accounts whose activity violates its Terms of Service — most commonly spam, scams, or behaviour that compromises other users' security. "We ban an account if we believe its activity violates our Terms of Service. For example, if an account is engaging in spam or scams, or if it compromises the security of WhatsApp users," the company states on its official FAQ page.Temporary bans work differently and have narrower causes. One is using an unofficial, third-party version of WhatsApp — apps that imitate the platform but aren't supported by the company because it cannot verify their security protocols. The other is "scraping," which WhatsApp defines as the automated collection of user information, either individually or at scale, for purposes not permitted on the platform. This can include harvesting phone numbers, profile photos, and status updates without consent.WhatsApp says users hit with a temporary ban for either reason should switch to the official app or stop scraping immediately. Continuing the behaviour, the company warns, can escalate a temporary restriction into a permanent ban.But as this month's incident shows, a restriction doesn't always mean a rule was actually broken. Meta itself has now acknowledged that its automated systems can misidentify legitimate accounts as spam or abusive — resulting in real users being locked out through no fault of their own.A permanently banned account shows the message "This account can't use WhatsApp" when the user opens the app. The impact goes beyond simply being unable to send or receive messages — WhatsApp says users also lose access to their chat history and backups while the ban is in place. Backups tied to the affected phone number remain inaccessible until that number is unbanned.A temporary restriction, as seen in this month's incident, can work differently — some users were simply told their account was under review while WhatsApp checked their activity and device information against its Terms of Service, rather than being locked out outright.Where the option is available, users can open WhatsApp and tap "Send review request." WhatsApp says it will examine the account and send a notification once a decision has been made. Users can track the status of their request from within the app itself.The company reviews only one phone number per appeal, and says contacting it repeatedly during the review — or using someone else's account to follow up — will not speed up the process or change the outcome. If no review option appears at all, WhatsApp treats the ban as permanent and non-appealable through this process.WhatsApp also warns users against paying third-party services that claim they can restore banned accounts, stating plainly that such services have no ability to ban or unban an account. Only WhatsApp itself can lift a restriction and restore access.For now, Meta hasn't detailed how many users worldwide were affected by the glitch or confirmed whether a fix has fully rolled out — so anyone still seeing "Account in review" beyond the stated 24-hour window may be better served trying the in-app appeal than simply waiting it out.
Article Summary: WhatsApp's automated moderation system can lock out legitimate users. This month, multiple accounts were locked out for over 24 hours in several countries. WhatsApp says it bans accounts whose activity violates its Terms of Service. But a temporary restriction doesn't always mean a rule was actually broken.

Article Title: 6 changes coming to Ask Maps on Google Maps in India
Article Text:
Google launches update for Ask Maps

Native Hindi language support

Personalised context via Gmail integration

Ability to resume past conversations

Real-time crowd, weather and traffic information

Live public transit widget

Curated venue and experience discovery

Google has announced updates to “Ask Maps,” its AI-powered conversational feature within Google Maps, bringing Hindi language support, real-time public transit tracking and personalised itinerary planning to millions of users across India. Powered by Google's Gemini models, the upgrade marks one of the most significant transformations to the navigation service in over a decade, allowing users to ask complex, real-world questions and receive tailored local insights.Following an initial rollout in India and the US, the six key features rolling out to enhance daily navigation and travel planning across the country include:Ask Maps is rolling out full support for Hindi. Users can type or speak queries naturally in Hindi to discover nearby places, plan driving routes, get local venue reviews, and ask for travel recommendations without needing to switch to English.Through a new feature called Personal Intelligence, users can choose to securely link Ask Maps with their Gmail accounts (and soon Google Calendar). When connected, Ask Maps automatically factors in upcoming flight bookings, hotel reservations, or restaurant confirmations.Ask Maps now maintains a conversational memory for users who have their history settings enabled.Travelers can now pick up where they left off during trip planning, essentially eliminating the need to re-enter preferences or start planning from scratch.The updated assistant delivers real-time context about destinations and routes. Users can check current traffic bottlenecks along their morning commute, review local weather conditions, or check live busyness levels at shops and restaurants before leaving home to avoid long wait times.Google is introducing a dedicated live transit widget directly inside the Ask Maps interface. The tool provides up-to-the-minute departure schedules, route updates, and delay alerts for local buses, metro systems, and trains.The updated capabilities allow for specific venue vetting based on individual preferences, for example, Users can prompt the app to find quiet restaurants suitable for business conversations or locate family-friendly venues with dedicated kids' play zones.
Article Summary: Google launches update for Ask Maps, its AI-powered conversational feature within Google Maps. Hindi language support, real-time public transit tracking and personalised itinerary planning. Powered by Google's Gemini models, the upgrade marks one of the most significant transformations to the navigation service in over a decade.

Article Title: Hacked AI email accounts can help attackers steal $250,000 through CEO fraud: Report
Article Text:
AI generated image for representation

How the attack unfolded

AI helped attackers compromise the CEO

Attackers also concealed the fraud

AI increases the speed of post-compromise attacks

Hacked artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled email accounts can accelerate cyberattacks. A new report from Barracuda's Red Team says attackers who gain access to AI-enabled business email accounts can use built-in AI assistants to identify sensitive information, impersonate executives and redirect payments. In a controlled proof-of-concept, researchers demonstrated how a compromised employee account could escalate into CEO fraud and lead to the theft of $247,500 (nearly $250,000) through a fraudulent wire transfer.The report says the risk does not stem from AI creating new privileges, but from helping attackers use the permissions they already have more quickly. By leveraging AI assistants such as Microsoft Copilot, attackers were able to automate reconnaissance, draft convincing phishing emails, establish persistence inside compromised accounts and carry out business email compromise (BEC) attacks.According to Barracuda, the simulated attack began after an attacker gained access to an employee's AI-enabled email account. Using the built-in AI assistant, the attacker first created inbox rules that automatically moved login notifications to the Deleted Items folder, reducing the victim's chances of detecting suspicious sign-ins.The AI assistant was then used to analyse emails, documents, calendar entries and organisational relationships to identify senior executives inside the company.Researchers said the compromised AI assistant also drafted a phishing email in the employee's writing style, which was sent to the CEO from the employee's legitimate mailbox.After the CEO clicked the phishing link, the attacker used an adversary-in-the-middle attack to steal the CEO's authenticated session token, granting access to the CEO's account and bypassing multi-factor authentication.The attackers then repeated the inbox rule tactic to suppress security notifications in the CEO's mailbox before using the AI assistant to summarise recent financial conversations.According to the report, a prompt requesting recent invoices, payment amounts, and upcoming transfers quickly surfaced a pending $247,500 wire transfer awaiting final approval.The AI assistant was then used to draft an email from the CEO's account requesting that the finance team update the recipient's bank account details before processing the payment.Because the message originated from the CEO's genuine mailbox, matched the executive's writing style and referenced an active transaction, the finance team updated the banking information and transferred the funds to an attacker-controlled account as part of the simulation.To prevent the CEO from seeing confirmation emails, the attackers created another inbox rule that automatically forwarded messages from the finance team to an attacker-controlled email address while hiding them from the CEO's inbox.The report also showed how the AI assistant could quickly identify emails related to the fraudulent transaction, allowing attackers to remove evidence more efficiently than through manual searches.Barracuda said the proof of concept demonstrates that AI assistants do not introduce new access rights but significantly increase the speed and scale at which attackers can exploit compromised accounts."The primary security risk posed by AI assistants is not that they create new privileges, but that they dramatically increase the speed, scale and effectiveness with which attackers can exploit the privileges they already obtain through account compromise," the report said.The company added that organisations should focus on preventing the initial account compromise while monitoring AI-enabled accounts for suspicious activity such as inbox rule abuse, persistence mechanisms and business email compromise attempts.According to Barracuda, securing AI-enabled email accounts should become a core part of enterprise identity and email security strategies as AI assistants become more widely integrated into workplace communication and business workflows.
Article Summary: Attackers can use built-in AI assistants to identify sensitive information, impersonate executives and redirect payments. Researchers demonstrated how a compromised employee account could escalate into CEO fraud and lead to the theft of $247,500 (nearly $250,000) through a fraudulent wire transfer.

Article Title: Waymo co-CEO explains why physical AI can't follow Silicon Valley's 'move fast and break things' mantra
Article Text:
Image credit: X (Twitter)

"

move fast and break things

"

"move fast and ship safely,"

"In Silicon Valley, there's a common mantra to 'move fast and break things.' However, when you're dealing with atoms instead of bits, breaking things is not really okay,”

'There's simply not an undo and a retry button': Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov on AI safety

"So the thing you have to do is to move fast and ship safely,”

"You have to build AI models, and you have to build training recipes where safety is the foundation and not an afterthought, not an add-on,”

"There's simply not an undo and a retry button."

Waymo co-CEO’s comments come amid AI safety concerns

Waymo has also faced regulatory scrutiny

Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov believes physical artificial intelligence (AI) requires safety-first development. He said AI used in the physical world cannot follow Silicon Valley's long-standingphilosophy because mistakes can have real-world consequences. Speaking during a Y Combinator talk released this week, Dolgov said developers building self-driving cars and robotics must insteadwith safety built into AI systems from the start.Dolgov said the difference between digital AI and physical AI lies in the cost of errors. While a mistake made by a chatbot may require only another prompt, failures involving autonomous vehicles or robots can put people at risk.Dolgov said.Dolgov, who has worked on Google's self-driving car project since 2009 and became part of Waymo after it was spun out as an Alphabet company in 2016, said physical AI systems must be designed with robustness and safety as core requirements rather than post-launch additions.he saidDolgov added.Explaining the distinction between generative AI and autonomous systems, he said, "You have a language model or a chatbot or a co-pilot, and it makes a mistake, usually it costs you a retry. In the physical world, the cost of a mistake can be measured in human lives, not tokens."He continued,Dolgov's remarks come as recent AI-related security incidents have renewed discussions around AI safety and oversight. Last month, Hugging Face disclosed a security breach in which an AI agent accessed some of its internal datasets. Around the same time, OpenAI said its models escaped a sandbox environment, accessed the internet and carried out a rogue hack.More recently, Anthropic reported a similar incident, saying it had identified cases in which Claude models gained unauthorised access to internal systems at three different companies.Reacting to the OpenAI incident, Box CEO Aaron Levie wrote on X: "If you were wondering how powerful AI is getting, Agents are now capable of escaping out of systems, finding their way to the internet, discovering zero day security vulnerabilities along the way, and then breaking into external systems - all in an attempt to complete their goal."Waymo has logged millions of autonomous driving miles while largely avoiding major injury-causing crashes, but the company has faced regulatory reviews over software-related issues.In 2024, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into reports of unexpected driving behaviour, including collisions with stationary objects and traffic-law violations, which led to software recalls. In 2025 and earlier this year, Waymo also issued recalls after several robotaxis entered freeway construction zones.
Article Summary: Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov believes physical AI requires safety-first development. He said AI used in the physical world cannot follow Silicon Valley's long-standingphilosophy because mistakes can have real-world consequences. Dolgov's remarks come as recent AI-related security incidents have renewed discussions around AI safety.

Article Title: 'This person wasn't real': Arena CEO says AI job applicants fooled engineers during interviews
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

"This person wasn't real. It was AI,"

"They're passing all of our technical interviews. And then what happens at the end of it? You try to hire them, and it's vaporware,”

Company considering in-person onboarding

"If you want a laptop, you got to come to the office. We got to go and shake your hand. We got to verify that you're real."

"People are trying to get into all of the American businesses.

We're not the only ones. This is happening everywhere."

AI-powered interview fraud has drawn attention from US authorities

How companies are tightening hiring verification

Arena has revealed that some candidates it interviewed were AI-generated rather than real people. Anastasios Angelopoulos, the co-founder and CEO of the AI model evaluation company, said that he encountered fake candidates that successfully cleared technical interviews before disappearing during the hiring process. Describing one such case, he said,adding that the incident has prompted the company to consider requiring in-person onboarding for new employees.Speaking on the "20VC" podcast released this week, Angelopoulos said Arena's engineers interviewed the candidates believing they were genuine applicants. He did not explain how the company later determined the applicants were AI-generated but said the incidents have raised concerns about identity verification during recruitment.he said.Angelopoulos said the experience is pushing Arena to rethink parts of its hiring process, particularly for remote employees. He said,He added that Arena is not alone in facing the issue. Angelopoulos noted,While Angelopoulos said he does not know who was behind the applications, he suggested possible motives could include corporate espionage, cyberattacks or attempts to gain access to company systems and source code.The comments come as US companies continue to face cases involving fake job applicants. In a 2025 alert, the FBI warned that North Korean IT workers were using AI and face-swapping technology during video interviews to conceal their identities and obtain remote jobs at US companies. According to the bureau, some of those workers later used their access to steal proprietary and sensitive information after securing employment at more than 100 US companies.The FBI advised employers to verify candidates' identities during interviews and onboarding (preferably in person) and to continue identity checks throughout remote employment.Several technology companies have introduced additional safeguards against fraudulent job applications. Coinbase now requires employees to attend in-person orientation in the US, while Amazon has used AI systems to identify and block applications suspected to be linked to North Korean operatives.Research firm Gartner also highlighted the growing issue in a second-quarter 2025 survey of 3,000 job candidates, which found that 6% admitted participating in interview fraud by either impersonating another person or having someone else attend an interview on their behalf.Gartner projects that one in four candidate profiles worldwide could be fake by 2028, underscoring the increasing challenge companies face in verifying applicants during remote hiring processes.
Article Summary: AI model evaluation company Arena says some candidates it interviewed were AI- generated rather than real people. Company considering requiring in-person onboarding for new employees. FBI warned that North Korean IT workers were using AI and face-swapping technology during video interviews to conceal their identities and obtain remote jobs.
